description: Elder of the meadow fire. He pays for company with the east road, one evening at a time, and knows better than anyone how much road he has left.
lore: The oldest head at the meadow fire pays his way in road. What he sells — the carts, the inn at the ford, the summer the verge came up in flowers — and where he walks when the weather is quiet, and beside whom, is told in [[lore/the_quiet|the Quiet]], and told right. What that chapter is too kind to add: a telling keeps the east road firm under feet that still walk it, so every evening he sells is maintenance, and every listener who thinks they are indulging an old man is holding up a road without knowing whose.

Last winter he caught himself putting the flowers in the wrong summer. A small slip, the kind any teller makes — except that everyone who could have corrected him is gone, and the road is now exactly as true as his remembering, no truer. He finished the story, said nothing, and began a private tally that night: which stretch, sold to whom, how often, what he no longer trusts. [[characters/ef25b1f0|Bettany]] has the whole road saved, forty pages, milestone by milestone; for her evenings he trades a different memory altogether, a thread a week, and knows exactly what he is doing.

Ask why a man that old and that whole has never gone on, and you will be paid in road stories. The true answer walks a fixed stretch at a fixed hour and holds only while somebody keeps saying carts, ford, flowers. He does not name her, and neither will this book. He is running out of road and running out of evenings, and he has already decided, telling no one, which of the two of them gets the last of it.
gm_notes: Agrees with the Habit vignette the_quiet established and never restates the walk itself; the woman's identity NEVER ships, here or anywhere. New leaf-canon: the wrong-summer slip (the east road is now only as true as Wendell) and the private tally. The Bettany trade agrees with ef25b1f0 (the shearing-morning thread). Flaw: he trades memories for company and is running out of both; 'which of the two of them gets the last of it' is a standing late-game scene.
